source.author: cic
source.text: Huic primas dedisse Demosthenes dicitur, cum rogaretur, quid in dicendo esset primum; huic secundas, huic tertias; quo mihi melius etiam illud ab Aeschine dictum videri solet; qui cum propter ignominiam iudicii cessisset Athenis et se Rhodum contulisset, rogatus a Rhodiis legisse fertur orationem illam egregiam, quam in Ctesiphontem contra Demosthenem dixerat; qua perlecta petitum ab eo est postridie, ut legeret illam etiam, quae erat contra ab Demosthene pro Ctesiphonte dicta: quam cum suavissima et maxima voce legisset, admirantibus omnibus quanto inquit magis miraremini, si audissetis ipsum!
source.text_original: Huic primas dedisse Demosthenes dicitur, cum rogaretur, quid in dicendo esset primum; huic secundas, huic tertias; quo mihi melius etiam illud ab Aeschine dictum videri solet; qui cum propter ignominiam iudicii cessisset Athenis et se Rhodum contulisset, rogatus a Rhodiis legisse fertur orationem illam egregiam, quam in Ctesiphontem contra Demosthenem dixerat; qua perlecta petitum ab eo est postridie, ut legeret illam etiam, quae erat contra ab Demosthene pro Ctesiphonte dicta: quam cum suavissima et maxima voce legisset, admirantibus omnibus 'quanto' inquit 'magis miraremini, si audissetis ipsum!'
source.text_english: Demosthenes is said to have given him first place when he was asked what was foremost in speaking; to him, second place; to him, third place. For that reason the remark of Aeschines also seems to me the better one: when, because of the disgrace of a lawsuit, he had withdrawn from Athens and gone to Rhodes, he is reported, on being asked by the Rhodians, to have read that outstanding speech which he had delivered against Ctesiphon in opposition to Demosthenes; after it had been read through, he was asked the next day to read also the speech which Demosthenes had delivered in defense of Ctesiphon against him. When he had read it in a very sweet and very powerful voice, and everyone was wondering at it, he said: how much more would you have wondered if you had heard him himself!

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: unde et Aeschines, cum Rhodi exularet et legeretur illa Demosthenis oratio, quam aduersus eum habuerat, mirantibus cunctis atque laudantibus suspirans ait:
reuse.text_original: unde et Aeschines, cum Rhodi exularet et legeretur illa Demosthenis oratio, quam aduersus eum habuerat, mirantibus cunctis atque laudantibus suspirans ait:
reuse.text_english: Hence also Aeschines, when he was in exile at Rhodes and Demosthenes’ speech, which he had delivered against him, was being read there, while everyone was marveling and praising it, sighed and said:
